en: The Śukarahasya Upaniṣad
Oṃ. May He protect us both; may He nourish us both; may we exert our strength together; may our study be luminous; may we never harbor hatred toward one another.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the Rahasyopaniṣad.
The celestial sages, having worshipped and prostrated before Brahmā, asked: "O Blessed One, please tell us the secret Upaniṣad. || 2 ||
In former times, Vyāsa, of great splendor and a treasure-house of all Vedas and asceticism, prostrated before Śiva with Ambā and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke as follows. (3)
Śrī Vedavyāsa said: O God of gods, O one of great wisdom, O you whose firm vow is the severing of bonds, [regarding] the rite of Vedic consecration for my son Śuka— || 4 ||
The time for the instruction of Brahman has now arrived; O Teacher of the World, the instruction of Brahman must be imparted by you today.
Īśvara said: "When Kaivalya, the eternal Brahman itself, has been taught by me, my son, having abandoned [all else] out of world-weariness, will himself attain illumination."
Śrī Vedavyāsa said: "In whatever manner it may be regarding the rite of initiation, since my son has been instructed in the Veda through your grace,"
O Maheśvara, may my son quickly become omniscient; endowed with your grace, may he attain the fourfold liberation.
Having heard those words of Vyāsa in the assembly of all the gods and sages, Śambhu, together with Sāmba, joyfully took his place upon a divine throne to provide instruction.
Having accomplished his purpose, Śuka, filled with great devotion, returned there; and having received the Praṇava from him, he spoke thus again to Śiva: || 10 ||
Śrī Śuka said: O God of gods, omniscient one, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss; O beloved of Umā, Lord of beings, O ocean of compassion, be gracious!
The supreme Parabrahman, which resides within the Praṇava, has been taught specifically through such statements as "That thou art" (tattvamasi) and by means of wisdom and other faculties.
O Sadāśiva, I desire to hear the six ancillaries (ṣaḍaṅga) in their true essence and in their proper order; please tell me these secrets today out of compassion. (13)
The illustrious Sadāśiva said: "Excellent, excellent, O highly wise Śuka, O sage, treasury of knowledge! You have asked what ought to be asked—a secret that contains the essence of the Vedas."
It is here declared by the name *Rahasyopaniṣad*, together with its six ancillaries; by the mere knowledge of which liberation is attained directly, without a doubt. (15)

The Guru should not again teach sentences that are deficient in their constituent parts; rather, he should teach the Great Sentences (Mahāvākyas) in their entirety, together with their six ancillaries (Ṣaḍaṅgas). || 16 ||
Just as among all four Vedas the Upanishads are the head, so too this Rahasyopanishad is the head of the Upanishads.

For that wise man by whom Brahman has been meditated upon according to the Rahasyopanishad, what need is there for pilgrimages, sacred mantras, scriptural studies, or recitations that serve as causes of merit? (18)

Whatever one obtains by reflecting on the meaning of the sentence for a hundred autumns, that same result is attained by reciting it just once while meditating upon the seers and other [constituent elements]. (19)

Oṃ. Of this great mantra of the Śrī Mahāvākya, Haṃsa is the seer (ṛṣi); the unmanifest Gāyatrī is the meter (chandaḥ); Paramahaṃsa is the deity (devatā); Haṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja); Saḥ is the power (śakti); So’haṃ is the pin (kīlaka). My application (viniyoga) is for the recitation of the Mahāvākyas for the sake of pleasing Paramahaṃsa. To Brahman, who is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite, salutation with both thumbs (aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ). To Brahman, who is Eternal Bliss, Svāhā with both index fingers (tarjanībhyāṃ svāhā). To Brahman, who consists of Eternal Bliss, Vaṣaṭ with both middle fingers (madhyamābhyāṃ vaṣaṭ).

To the *bhūman* (the Infinite), with the two ring fingers: *hum*. To the Lord of the *bhūman*, with the two little fingers: *vauṣaṭ*. To Brahman, who is one alone without a second, with the palms and backs of the hands: *phaṭ*. "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite"—to the heart: *namaḥ*. "Brahman is Eternal Bliss"—to the head: *svāhā*. "Brahman consists of Eternal Bliss"—to the tuft of hair (*śikhā*): *vaṣaṭ*. To the *bhūman*, with the armor (*kavaca*): *hum*. To the Lord of the *bhūman*, to the three eyes: *vauṣaṭ*.
To Brahman, who is one alone without a second, to the weapon (*astra*): *phaṭ*. "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ"—thus is the binding of the directions (*digbandha*). || 20 ||

I bow to that True Guru—meditation itself, eternal bliss, the bestower of supreme happiness, the embodiment of absolute knowledge, transcending the universe, resembling the sky, the goal indicated by "That Thou Art" and other Great Sayings; who is one, eternal, stainless, immovable, the witness of all intellects, beyond all mental states, and devoid of the three qualities. 21.
Now, the four great sayings (*mahāvākya*s). As follows:
"Oṃ, consciousness is Brahman" (1).
Oṃ, I am Brahman. 2.
Oṃ, that thou art. || 3 ||
Oṃ, this Self is Brahman. || 4 ||
Those who recite this expression of non-difference, "That thou art" (tattvamasi), become partakers of liberation through union with Śiva. || 22 ||

For this great mantra of the *Tat-pada*: the *ṛṣi* is Paramahaṃsa; the meter (*chandas*) is the Unmanifest Gāyatrī; the deity (*devatā*) is Paramahaṃsa; *haṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*); *saḥ* is the power (*śakti*); *so’ham* is the pin (*kīlaka*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of recitation (*japa*) for my liberation through union (*sāyujya-mukti*). *Tatpuruṣāya*, to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*. *Īśānāya*, to the two index fingers, *svāhā*. *Aghorāya*, to the two middle fingers, *vaṣaṭ*. *Sadyojātāya*, to the two ring fingers, *hum*. *Vāmadevāya*, to the two little fingers, *vauṣaṭ*.

Salutation to Tatpuruṣa, Īśāna, Aghora, Sadyojāta, and Vāmadeva; *phaṭ* with the palms and the backs of the hands. Thus is the placement (*nyāsa*) of the heart and other limbs. *Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar om*—thus is the binding of the directions (*digbandha*). || 23 ||

One should meditate thus upon that radiant splendor: meditation itself; knowledge; the object of knowledge; that which transcends the reach of knowledge and so forth; pure, awakened, liberated, and imperishable; truth, knowledge, and the very form of being-consciousness-bliss. (24)

For the great mantra of the *tvaṃ*-word: Viṣṇu is the seer (*ṛṣi*); Gāyatrī is the meter (*chanda*); the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is the deity (*devatā*); *aiṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*); *klīṃ* is the power (*śakti*); *sauḥ* is the pin (*kīlaka*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is for my recitation (*japa*) for the sake of liberation. Salutation with both thumbs to Vāsudeva; *svāhā* with both index fingers to Saṅkarṣaṇa; *vaṣaṭ* with both middle fingers to Pradyumna; *hum* with both ring fingers to Aniruddha; *vauṣaṭ* with both little fingers to Vāsudeva.

To Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha, [I offer] with the palms and backs of the hands: *phaṭ*. Thus is the placement (*nyāsa*) of the heart and other limbs. With *bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar oṃ*, there is the binding of the directions (*digbandha*). || 25 ||
I worship the state known as the *jīva*, which is the meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) of all beings, whose form is unbroken everywhere, and who is the driver of the mind, ego, and the senses. (26)

For the great mantra of Asipada: the seer (ṛṣi) is Mana; the meter (chandas) is Gāyatrī; the deity (devatā) is Ardhanārīśvara; the seed-syllable (bīja) is the Unmanifest (avyakta) and so forth; the power (śakti) is Nṛsiṃha; the pin (kīlaka) is the Supreme Self (paramātman). The application (viniyoga) is in the recitation for the purpose of realizing the unity of the individual soul and Brahman. To the binary atom of earth, salutation with the two thumbs (aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ). To the binary atom of water, svāhā with the two index fingers (tarjanībhyāṃ svāhā). To the binary atom of fire, vaṣaṭ with the two middle fingers (madhyamābhyāṃ vaṣaṭ). To the binary atom of air, huṃ with the two ring fingers (anāmikābhyāṃ huṃ).

To the ether-dyad (ākāśadvyaṇuka), *vauṣaṭ* with the two little fingers. To earth, water, fire, air, and ether-dyads, *phaṭ* with the palms and backs of the hands. "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ oṃ"—thus is the binding of the directions (*digbandha*). || 27 ||

Meditation: As long as the mind remains fixed on the meaning of the statement "The individual soul (jīva) is Brahman," one should always meditate upon the state of being [the Self] (asipada), effecting the dissolution of the reality of duality into unity. 28.
Thus, the six limbs of the great statements have been explained. || 29 ||
Now, the verses concerning the meaning of the statements are being proclaimed according to the divisions of the Rahasyopaniṣad.
That by which one sees, hears this, smells, articulates, and discerns what is sweet and what is not sweet—that is declared to be *prajñāna*. (31)
In the four-faced Indra and the gods, and in humans, horses, cows, and so forth, consciousness is the one Brahman; therefore, "Brahman is pure consciousness" applies to me as well.
The supreme Self, fully complete within this body that is qualified for knowledge, abides as the witness of the intellect; manifesting itself, it is designated as "I. (33)
The Supreme Self, inherently full, is here described by the word "Brahman. Through the reflective awareness of oneness as "I am," I become that Brahman. (34)
"That which is one alone, without a second, and devoid of name and form—its very same nature is said to persist now as it was before creation. (35)
In this context, the word "thou" (tvaṃ) denotes a reality that transcends the body and senses of the listener; by [the use of] "this" (asi), oneness is grasped—let that identity be experienced. (36)
This [Self] is considered to be self-luminous and immediate based on the statement "this is I"; from the ego-sense up to the body, it is celebrated as the inner Self (pratyagātman). || 37 ||
The reality of the entire world as it is perceived is designated by the word "Brahman"; that Brahman has the nature of a self-luminous consciousness. (38)

Having fallen into the dream-state of "I" and "mine," which is the sleep of non-discrimination caused by the view of a self, I have now awakened through the clear words of the Great Sayings of the Guru, once the sun of my true nature has risen. (39)

The path of meaning is twofold: the expressed (*vācya*) and the indicated (*lakṣya*). Indeed, regarding the word "thou" (*tvam-pada*), that which is expressed consists of the physical body, the senses, and so forth; whereas that which is indicated is the true referent of "thou" (*tvam-artha*). Regarding the word "that" (*tat-pada*), the expressed is the notion of lordship (*īśatā*); however, the indicated is Brahman, which is Being-Consciousness-Bliss-Absolute (*sac-cid-ānanda-brahma*), and this is the true referent of "that" (*tad-artha*). The identity of these two is the state of "That art thou" (*tat-tvam-asi*).

When there is a cause and an effect, and when limiting adjuncts (upādhi) exist, there is this duality of "thou" and "that"; otherwise, it is one, whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss. Having abandoned both the words and their causes—namely space and time—it becomes one in the world, just as Devadatta is one and the same person.

This individual soul (jīva) has the effect as its limiting adjunct (upādhi), while the Lord (īśvara) has the cause as his limiting adjunct; having abandoned the state of being both cause and effect, pure, perfect consciousness remains.
First there is hearing from the guru, then reflection, and thereafter meditative absorption; this is the cause of perfect awakening. (43)

The thorough knowledge of any other science will necessarily be perishable; however, the thorough knowledge of the science of Brahman is established as that which brings about the attainment of Brahman. 44.
The teacher should instruct the great sayings (mahāvākyas) along with their six ancillaries (ṣaḍaṅgas); for the mere sayings alone are not the word of Brahman. 45.
Īśvara said: O Śuka, best of sages, having spoken thus, I—Vyāsa, the expounder of Brahman who was entreated by my father—[revealed] the secret Upaniṣad.
Then, constantly meditating upon that which was taught by Brahmā—the characteristic of which is Being-Consciousness-Bliss—you, being liberated while living, shall wander eternally.
That which is declared as the primal sound at the beginning of the Vedas and established at the end of the Vedas—He who is beyond that [sound] when it has dissolved into its source is Maheśvara.
Having been thus instructed by Śiva, he attained identity with the universe; then, rising and prostrating before the Lord, he renounced all possessions.
Then, as if floating upon the ocean of the Supreme Brahman, he departed; and seeing him thus going forth into the religious life, the sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana [spoke].
Following after him, he called out, distressed by the separation from his son; then all beings in the world, both mobile and immobile, responded to him.
Having heard that account in its entirety, Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, together with his son, attained supreme bliss out of affection.
Whoever studies this Rahasyopaniṣad through the grace of the guru, being liberated from all sins, attains manifest liberation—attains manifest liberation. Thus ends the Upaniṣad.
Oṃ. May He protect us both together; may He nourish us both together; may we work together with great vigor; may our study be brilliant; may we never harbor hatred toward one another.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace!
Thus ends the Śukarahasya Upaniṣad.
